summary.text: Hector and Ajax fought in single combat until nightfall and exchanged gifts, the armies buried their dead under truce — and on the next day Zeus turned the war against the Achaeans until the Trojans camped among the ships and the host built a wall with a trench before their camp.

chapters.title: Hector's challenge
chapters.text: When the battle stalled, Hector stepped forth and challenged the best of the Achaeans to single combat — the victor's side to take the day. Nine captains drew lots; the lot fell to Telamonian Ajax, bulwark of the host. The two heroes fought with spears and stones until heralds stopped them for night — equals in valour, though Hector had the edge in casting. They parted with gifts: Ajax gave a sword with silver studs, Hector a war-belt — guest-friendship between enemies for a single evening.

chapters.title: Burial under truce
chapters.text: Hector proposed a truce to burn the dead; the Achaeans agreed, and for one day Trojans and Danaans gathered their slain without battle. The Trojans burned their dead on the plain and raised a cairn; the Achaeans burned theirs and raised a barrow on the shore. It was the last calm before Zeus fulfilled Thetis' request in earnest — the gods would soon forbid open intervention, but the human cost of the war was already heaped on both sides.

chapters.title: Zeus turns the tide
chapters.text: On Olympus Zeus weighed the fates of Troy and Achaea in his golden scales; the Achaean side sank. He forbade gods and goddesses to join the field and drove the Trojans forward behind Hector. Agamemnon's aristeia failed before the storm; Diomedes and Odysseus were wounded; the Achaean line broke toward the ships. Nestor rallied the captains, but the day ended with the Trojans camped on the plain and watch-fires burning like stars along the ridges — Troy's best day while Achilles still sat idle.

chapters.title: The Achaean wall
chapters.text: That night the beaten host dug a trench and raised a wall with towers and gates — work they should have done at the war's beginning, Poseidon would later say. They drove stakes into the ditch and piled earth; the wall stood through the rest of the Iliad until Troy fell. The nested episode on the Embassy tells Book 9, when Agamemnon would try to buy Achilles back; here the story ends with the siege works that could not save the ships without the son of Peleus.
